A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CHARM research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: Sections 5 and Appendix C report original hallucination-detection experiments on five datasets, including comparative performance, ablations, transfer results, and runtime measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds activation-layer experiments, sequence-length analyses, and sample-level prediction visualizations.

M1.justification: Appendix C.2 adds an implemented CHARM variant concatenating activations from layers 24, 28, and 32. v1 evaluated single-layer activations and described multilayer inputs as future exploration. The graph construction, message-passing architecture, pooling, and prediction procedure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use NQ, CNN, Movies, WinoBias, and Math for the same detection tasks. The new length experiments analyze and repartition existing CNN samples; they do not introduce additional datasets, domains, or underlying task coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged, including P(True) and Semantic Entropy in Appendix C.1. New appendix experiments reuse activation probes and Lookback Lens. The newly cited ACT-ViT work is not evaluated as a baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix C.3 adds a CNN split reserving the longest 20% of sequences for testing, plus length-binned resource and performance evaluations. Appendix C.2 adds activation configurations. Appendix D.3 corrects the reported Mistral checkpoint from v0.3 to v0.2, explicitly identifying a reporting error rather than establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendices C.2–C.3 substantially extend supplementary analysis with activation-layer sensitivity and combination tests, runtime and memory scaling, accuracy by length, and training-short/testing-long robustness. Appendix E also adds two NQ examples showing graph structure, labels, and predictions. These address questions beyond v1's graph-removal, sparsification, and cross-dataset analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report CHARM performance as means and standard deviations over three training seeds. v2 Figure 3 additionally reports median runtime and memory consumption with interquartile ranges within length bins. This adds a variability-summary practice without documenting an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–6 are unchanged. Targeted additions include Math results for layer-28 and joint-layer inputs, with the latter scoring 82.7 ± 0.1 AUROC and 84.0 ± 0.5 AUPR, and CNN long-sequence results of 74.5 ± 0.7 and 21.6 ± 1.2, respectively. Figures 3–4 add length-dependent findings. These are new configurations and evaluations, not improvements to unchanged experimental settings.

T1.justification: The graph definitions, architectural equations, two expressiveness propositions, assumptions, and Appendix A proofs retain the same mathematical content. Differences are formatting, citation style, and pagination.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: computational traces as attributed graphs, CHARM's expressiveness, strong detection performance, and promising cross-dataset transfer. Added supporting experiments do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendices C.2–C.3 newly interpret CHARM as robust to activation-layer choice, potentially benefiting from combining layers, and relatively insensitive to sequence length within the tested range. They also connect favorable resource scaling to sparsified message passing. Existing interpretations and qualifications concerning cross-dataset transfer remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v2 supplies a repository address and states that training and evaluation scripts are available. v2 also corrects the Mistral checkpoint identification and documents the new layer-concatenation and length-analysis procedures. Existing hardware, optimizer, and hyperparameter-grid information is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Bar-Shalom et al.'s ACT-ViT work to the activation-based detection discussion and references. Other prominent bibliography changes update publication metadata or titles of retained works. The positioning relative to attention heuristics and graph-based learning remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 reorders the research questions, expands the Section 5.3 roadmap, adds appendix subsections, and moves the hyperparameter material from C.2 to C.4 and the LLM-usage statement from E to F. Citation style, headings, and conference identification also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds two experimental tables and four figures: resource-scaling plots, length-binned performance plots, and two full-page graph/prediction visualizations. It also adopts the ICLR layout, changing typography and placement of existing displays. Original Figures 1–2 and Tables 1–6 are retained; the hyperparameter table is renumbered.

improvement.justification: The added activation-choice and sequence-length analyses provide useful evidence about robustness and practical scaling that v1 lacked. Correcting the checkpoint identification and supplying concrete code-access information also improve reproducibility. These are valuable, targeted gains around an otherwise retained method, theoretical foundation, and principal experimental results.
